# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The transvenous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) has been a cornerstone of sudden cardiac death (SCD) prevention for decades [1]. However, complications related to transvenous leads—including lead fracture, insulation failure, venous occlusion, and systemic infection—remain a significant source of long-term morbidity [2,3]. The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to circumvent these limitations by avoiding intravascular and intracardiac hardware entirely [4]. This review summarizes the development, evidence base, indications, limitations, and future directions of S-ICD therapy.

## Device Design and Evolution

The S-ICD consists of a pulse generator implanted in the left lateral thoracic region and a single subcutaneous electrode positioned parasternally [4]. The initial proof-of-concept work by Bardy and colleagues established that defibrillation could be reliably achieved without transvenous components, identifying the optimal electrode configuration through systematic comparative testing [4]. The first-generation device received CE mark approval in 2009 and US Food and Drug Administration approval in 2012 [5]. Subsequent generations reduced device size, improved battery longevity, and refined sensing algorithms to reduce inappropriate shocks [6,7].

## Sensing and Detection

Unlike transvenous systems that sense intracardiac electrograms, the S-ICD uses surface-like vectors, making accurate rhythm discrimination more challenging [8]. Three sensing vectors are available, and an automated screening process—either with a paper template or an automated screening tool—is performed before implantation to ensure adequate R-wave sensing and minimize T-wave oversensing [9]. Patients with inadequate screening are not suitable candidates [9]. The morphology-based discrimination algorithms have been progressively refined to distinguish ventricular arrhythmias from supraventricular arrhythmias and to reduce oversensing [10].

## Clinical Evidence

Early clinical experience was reported in the IDE study and the EFFORTLESS registry, which demonstrated high conversion efficacy for induced ventricular fibrillation and acceptable complication rates [5,11]. Pooled analyses of these cohorts confirmed effective termination of spontaneous and induced ventricular arrhythmias [12]. The PRAETORIAN trial was the pivotal randomized controlled trial comparing S-ICD with transvenous ICD in patients without pacing indications [13]. It demonstrated non-inferiority of the S-ICD for the composite endpoint of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks, with fewer lead-related complications offset by more non-lead-related issues [13]. The UNTOUCHED study specifically evaluated inappropriate shock rates with contemporary programming and demonstrated low rates comparable to transvenous systems [14].

Inappropriate shocks, historically a concern, are most commonly caused by T-wave oversensing and supraventricular tachycardia [15]. Dual-zone programming and software upgrades have substantially reduced these events [16]. Registry data have consistently confirmed the absence of systemic lead-related infections and the relative ease of device extraction compared with transvenous leads [17,18].

## Indications and Patient Selection

The S-ICD is indicated for patients requiring ICD therapy who do not need bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or antitachycardia pacing (ATP) [19]. It is particularly attractive in young patients with long anticipated device lifespans, those with channelopathies such as Brugada syndrome and long QT syndrome, patients with prior device infections, and those with limited vascular access [20,21]. Guidelines from professional societies have incorporated the S-ICD as a recommended option in appropriately selected patients [19,22]. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy may also benefit, though T-wave oversensing risk warrants careful screening [23].

## Limitations

The principal limitations are the inability to provide long-term bradycardia pacing, ATP, or resynchronization [24]. ATP is valuable for painlessly terminating monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, and its absence may lead to more shocks in patients prone to such arrhythmias [25]. The S-ICD generator is larger and delivers higher-energy shocks (80 J) than transvenous devices, and implant-site discomfort and erosion have been reported [26]. Defibrillation testing remains recommended at implantation in many centers [27].

## Future Directions

A major advance is the combination of the S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker to provide ATP and pacing through modular communication, addressing the principal therapeutic gap [28]. The MODULAR ATP study has reported early feasibility of such communicating systems [28]. Refinements in implantation technique, including the intermuscular two-incision approach, have improved cosmesis and reduced complications [29]. Ongoing efforts focus on improved discrimination algorithms, smaller devices, and better patient-selection tools to optimize outcomes [30].

## Conclusion

The S-ICD represents a significant advance in SCD prevention by eliminating transvenous lead-related complications. Robust randomized and registry evidence supports its efficacy and safety in appropriately selected patients without pacing needs. Integration with leadless pacing technology promises to broaden its applicability, positioning the S-ICD as an increasingly versatile component of the defibrillation armamentarium.
